chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Abdullah ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from al-Husayn ibn Abi al-A'ala, who said:
I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'What is permissible for a man from the wealth of his son?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'His subsistence without extravagance, when he is in need of it.'

He (the narrator) said, 'So I said to him, 'What about the words of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) to the man who came to him and presented his father, so he (peace be upon him) said to him: 'You and your wealth are for your father'? He (peace be upon him) said: 'Rather, he came with his father to the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family), so he said, 'O Messenger of Allah! This is my father, and he has been unjust to me regarding my inheritance from my mother.' So the father informed him that he had spent it upon him and upon himself. So he (peace be upon him) said: 'You and your wealth are for your father', and there was not anything with the man; would the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) have withheld the father for the sake of the son?'
ai.seo_question: What is a father's right to his son's wealth in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq clarifies that a father's right to his son's wealth is limited to necessary subsistence without extravagance, distinguishing it from absolute ownership. This is contextualized by the Prophet's declaration 'You and your wealth are for your father,' which Shia scholars interpret as referring to a specific case where the father had already consumed the son's inheritance, thereby establishing the principle of need-based entitlement rather than perpetual claim.
